title: Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co. (1949)
summary: Filing under Federal Rule 3 did not substitute for the service necessary to satisfy the state limitations rule.
notes:
The casebook provides the historical filing and service sequence. Its core role is the distinction between federal commencement and state limitations tolling, not a universal rule that state service methods control in federal court.

The accident occurred in Kansas on October 1, 1943; Ragan filed in the District of Kansas on September 4, 1945 and served the summons on December 28, 1945, after Kansas's two-year period; the district court denied summary judgment and a verdict was entered for Ragan, the Tenth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed in an opinion by Justice Douglas, with Justice Rutledge dissenting.

The Court's rationale was that a state-created cause of action cannot be given longer life in federal court than it would have in state court; Walker v. Armco Steel (1980) reaffirmed Ragan after Hanna, reading Rule 3 as not addressing tolling of state limitations periods.

sections.Parties: Ragan sought recovery for an accident and faced a limitations defense from the defendant.
sections.Material Facts: The complaint was filed in federal court before the state limitations period ended, but service occurred later than permitted by the state rule for commencing the action for limitations purposes. Rule 3 stated when a federal action commenced; the contested point was whether that filing alone preserved the state-law claim.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court applied the state rule and rejected the argument that Federal Rule 3 alone saved the claim.
sections.Issue: Did Rule 3 displace the state service requirement connected to the statute of limitations?
sections.Holding: No. The federal rule did not govern the particular tolling question in the manner asserted.
sections.Reasoning: The Court treated the state commencement requirement as linked to the time within which the state right could be enforced. Merely identifying a federal rule using the word “commence” did not establish that it answered the same question. Walker later expressly revisits this interpretation after Hanna.

learning.why: Filing under Federal Rule 3 did not substitute for the service necessary to satisfy the state limitations rule.

topics.cp-rule-scope: Federal Rule 3 did not determine when the state limitations period was tolled.
topics.cp-limitations: The state service requirement governed timely enforcement of the state-created claim.
topics.cp-erie-outcome: Ragan applies York's outcome-determination test to a state rule on when an action is commenced for limitations purposes.
topics.cp-erie: The holding rests on Erie's principle that a state claim cannot have longer life in federal court than in state court.

mnemonic.rationale: Served after the state period ran
